title: A stranger's sojourn
hookLine: life is a war and a traveler's stay; what can guide us? philosophy (Meditations 2.17)

cards: How do you get through a life that won't hold still? Marcus Aurelius ends his second book by piling up pictures of how short and slippery it is. A point.
A river. A dream, and smoke. It reads like one long breath out.
Then, at the bottom of the pile, he asks a single question: what can guide a person through all this? Today: a stranger's sojourn.

teach.h: A POINT, A RIVER, A DREAM.
teach.b: Section seventeen begins: the time of a human life is a point. Its substance is always flowing. The senses are dim, the body decaying, the soul a whirl.
Fortune is hard to read, and fame is without judgment. Everything of the body is a river; everything of the soul, a dream and smoke. Then comes the line in today's title.

teach.h: A WAR, AND A STRANGER'S STAY.
teach.b: In Long's translation: "life is a warfare and a stranger's sojourn, and after-fame is oblivion." A war, because it's struggle.
A stranger's sojourn, because we're travelers here, staying a while in a place that isn't ours to keep.
Then the question: "What then is that which is able to conduct a man? One thing and only one, philosophy." For Marcus, philosophy wasn't a subject.

It was a way of living: keeping the spirit within unharmed, above pleasure and pain; doing nothing without aim and nothing false; not depending on what others do or don't do; accepting what comes; and meeting death calmly, as nature's work.
Listeners on this path will answer differently. Some are guided by a faith, some by a teacher, a text, a practice, a person. Marcus named his.
The question is the gift: if life is a traveler's stay, what are you traveling by?
So book two ends, and our week in it: stop spinning, mind your own mind, live ready to leave, see how fast things vanish, don't pry, don't wound yourself with anger.
A long list of what slips away, and one thing to hold on to.

how: Some readers of Marcus treat life as a stay in borrowed rooms, and keep a guide, philosophical or religious, that they return to each day.

games.q: you're Marcus at the end of book two. life is a point, the body a river, the soul a dream. what can guide a person?
games.why: "One thing and only one, philosophy": for him, a way of living, not a subject.

practice: Picture yourself as a traveler in a borrowed room: your body, your days, your people, none of it yours to keep and all of it yours to care for.
Ask quietly what guides you here, a faith, a teacher, a book, a practice, a person, a few hard-won rules, and name it. If you're not sure, that's honest too; sit with the question.

wordCard.voice: A stranger's sojourn. Marcus calls life a war and a traveler's stay, and asks what can guide us. For him, one thing: philosophy. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a stranger, a guest, a foreigner. Life, for Marcus, is a stranger's stay.

carryVoice: Your line: a traveler's stay. A borrowed room, and a guide for the road. Rest well.
